children.text: Water-hammer effect

A nonviscous liquid flows one-dimensionally in a rigid pipe of length L and radius R. A reservoir feeds its upstream end B at depth h below the free surface, and a valve at downstream end A opens to atmosphere Pa. Water has reference density ρ0=1000 kg/m³ and bulk modulus B=2.2 GPa, defined for the finite element by \(\Delta P=-B\Delta V/V_0\). Initially flow velocity is v0 in +x with pressure P0. A pressure front moves upstream at positive laboratory speed c. Valve closure changes downstream fluid velocity to v1≤0 in A. The short valve has opening radius r, cone angle β, and a contracted atmospheric jet of radius rc=r√Cc. Its inlet and contracted-jet streamlines are parallel. Contraction data (r/R,Cc at 45°,Cc at 90°) are (0,.746,.611),(.2,.747,.616),(.3,.748,.622),(.4,.749,.631),(1,1,1). For C and D treat c and ρ0 as constants, neglect valve length, use β=90° and use the incompressible steady-valve relation locally. In D additionally approximate reservoir pressure Ph by P0, as requested for the wave-reflection model, without resetting the given initial flow to zero.

children.text: Water-hammer effect
a.1. Wave pressure and speed

In the front frame continuity gives ρ0(c+v0)=ρ1(c+v1). Momentum gives ΔPs=−ρ0(c+v0)(v1−v0). The finite-volume modulus gives ΔPs=B(ρ1−ρ0)/ρ1. Combining yields c+v0=√(B/ρ0). Thus \(\alpha=-(1+v_0/c),\ \beta=-v_0,\ \gamma=1\). For v0≪c, c≈√(B/ρ0) and ΔPs≈−ρ0cΔv. A density-based linearized modulus changes higher-order terms, as discussed in the source.
a.2. Sudden-closure magnitude

The acoustic speed relative to water is √(B/ρ0)=1483 m/s, and the upstream laboratory front speed is 1479 m/s. At source precision c≈\(1.5\times10^{3}\) m/s. The pressure rise is v0√(ρ0B)≈5.93 MPa. The field checks the pressure in MPa.
b.1. Valve pressure relation

Continuity gives \(v_c=v_{in}R^2/(C_cr^2)\). Bernoulli between the parallel sections gives \[\Delta P_{in}=\frac{\rho_0v_{in}^2}{2}\left[\frac1{C_c^2}\left(\frac Rr\right)^4-1\right].\] This applies for nonzero opening, not at the fully closed limit with zero flow.
c.1. Fully open initial flow
At r=R, Cc=1 so inlet and outlet speeds agree and P0=Pa. Bernoulli from the reservoir free surface gives \(v_0=\sqrt{2gh}\).
c.2. First round trip after closure

Just before τ/2 the compression front has nearly reached B, leaving virtually the whole pipe at \(P=P_0+\rho_0cv_0\), v=0. The fixed-pressure reservoir reflects an expansion of amplitude Ph−P1. Just before τ the return front has nearly reached A, leaving \(P=P_h\) and \(v=-v_0+gh/c\). The infinitesimal regions ahead of each front retain the previous state. At the exact closed boundary velocity remains zero until the incoming front reflects, so the stated limits refer to the pipe interior.
d.1. Finite-step closure recursion

After each reservoir reflection, the arriving valve-side velocity is \(v_{n-1}-\Delta P_{n-1}/(\rho_0c)\). The next upstream wave therefore gives \[\frac{\Delta P_n}{\rho_0c}=v_{n-1}-v_n-\frac{\Delta P_{n-1}}{\rho_0c}.\] For n<4 set \(k_n=(R/r_n)^4/C_n^2-1\) and use ΔPn=ρ0knvn²/2. Thus \[\frac{k_n}{2c}v_n^2+v_n+\frac{\Delta P_{n-1}}{\rho_0c}-v_{n-1}=0.\] Choose the nonnegative root. For n=4 use v4=0 directly in the recursion.
d.2. Graphical pressure-velocity construction

Each step line is \(\Delta P=-X+X_{n-1}-\Delta P_{n-1}\). The valve parabola is \(\Delta P=k_nX^2/(2\rho_0c^2)\), with kn≈97.1,318,1646 for the first three openings. Starting at (6,0) MPa, intersections are approximately (5.37,0.624), (3.75,0.997), (1.695,1.06) and (0,0.643) MPa. The fourth curve is the vertical line X=0. Slow staged closure keeps these peaks well below the 6 MPa sudden-closure estimate. The source's first graphical table contains a mistyped 5.8 MPa coordinate, corrected by its appendix to 5.37 MPa.
